overview: The Small Business Administration's (SBA) 504 loan program helps small businesses buy buildings, land, and major equipment through government-backed loans made with nonprofit community lenders called certified development companies. This bill would add new program goals, such as companies that run at least 12 weeks of job training, rebuilding areas hit by declared disasters (generally for five years), and growth of businesses with 10 or fewer workers. It would let experienced lenders make small fixes at closing, such as correcting typos or shifting up to 10 percent of project costs, without SBA approval, and let approved private attorneys handle closing paperwork for top-rated lenders while an SBA risk office takes over file reviews. It would also change how much of a financed building a business may rent out to tenants, allowing more leasing in some cases, with a lower bar for small manufacturers building new facilities, and with annual checks that the borrower isn't really a real estate developer. Finally, it would exempt 504 and other development company loans, as well as certain other SBA financing, from the rule that borrowers must show they can't get credit elsewhere, and require the SBA to market the program. As of October 9, 2026, a House committee had approved it and it was placed on the House calendar for a vote.
for: Supporters say the changes cut red tape and closing delays, make the program more useful to small manufacturers and very small firms, and encourage hiring and training.
against: Critics say dropping the requirement that borrowers can't get credit elsewhere, loosening leasing limits, and shifting closing reviews to private attorneys could steer federal backing toward businesses that don't need it and weaken oversight of taxpayer risk.
